note: Which layers this app uses, where each comes from, and what each can and cannot say. Layers are grouped by how the number is made, not ranked. Every row lists the documents it was written from.

sides.title: From space, or built by computer models
sides.blurb: Coverage and dates differ by layer. Each number describes a grid square or a pixel, rather than your exact field.

sides.title: Measured or surveyed on the ground
sides.blurb: These start from people and instruments in the field. Each one is a point or a map area, so it can only speak for its own surroundings.

sides.title: Not connected to this app
sides.blurb: These NASA layers are not shown and nothing is estimated in their place.

bothSides.title: Satellites and models cover everywhere
bothSides.text: NASA says its rain product IMERG is particularly valuable where there are no ground-based precipitation instruments. ECMWF notes that reanalyses are usually produced at lower resolution than current weather forecasts. So wide coverage comes with coarse squares.

cites.quote: IMERG is particularly valuable over areas of Earth's surface that lack ground-based precipitation-measuring instruments, including oceans and remote areas.
Reanalyses are usually produced at lower resolution than current weather forecasts, and they use the same modern data assimilation system and forecasting model throughout the reanalysis period.

bothSides.title: Ground measurements speak for one place
bothSides.text: A CIMIS station estimates evapotranspiration for the station location and its immediate surroundings. A well reading is a fact about that well. A CoCoRaHS gauge measures the rain one volunteer's gauge caught.

cites.quote: Most of the CIMIS stations produce estimates of reference evapotranspiration (ETo) for the station location and their immediate surroundings, often in agricultural areas.
CoCoRaHS is a unique, non-profit, community-based network of volunteers of all ages and backgrounds working together to measure and map precipitation (rain, hail, and snow).

bothSides.title: Each side leans on the other
bothSides.text: The Cropland Data Layer is made from satellite images but trained with ground field records. Daymet is a map, but it is built from weather station observations. GLDAS takes in both satellite and ground observations.

cites.quote: Agricultural training and validation data are derived from the Farm Service Agency (FSA) Common Land Unit (CLU) Program.

The Daymet approach to estimating daily surface weather parameters at locations lacking instrumentation is based on a combination of interpolation and extrapolation, using inputs from multiple instrumented sites and weights for each site that reflect the spatial and temporal relationships of the estimation location to the instrumental observations.

The goal of the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) is to ingest satellite- and ground-based observational data products, using advanced land surface modeling and data assimilation techniques, in order to generate optimal fields of land surface states and fluxes

layers.name: NASA POWER daily weather
layers.plain: Daily temperature, humidity, wind, sunlight and rain for any point on Earth. The weather comes from computer weather-model data and the sunlight from satellite observations.
layers.resolution: Weather: about half a degree of latitude by five-eighths of a degree of longitude (about 50 km). Sunlight: 1 degree by 1 degree. Daily.
layers.canSay: How hot, dry, windy and sunny a region was on each day, the same way for every place and every year. It is what lets the app replay 40 seasons anywhere.
layers.cannotSay: What happened on your field. It is a model of a whole grid square, and it can read differently from a station (for example on rain, below).
layers.statusText: Saved for the three demo pins; fetched live elsewhere. Always labelled 'regional climate, about 50 km grid'.

cites.quote: ½° latitude by ⅝° longitude for the meteorological data sets
That resolution is 1.0° latitude by 1.0° longitude for the radiation data sets
Meteorological parameters continue to be based upon MERRA-2 and GEOS FP-IT assimilation models.

layers.name: Landsat greenness (NDVI)
layers.plain: How green the ground looks from space, from the red and near-infrared light that plants reflect. The app follows the one 30 m pixel that contains your pin.
layers.resolution: 30 m pixel. Landsat 8 repeats every 16 days (Landsat 9 is offset by 8 days). Clear days only.
layers.coverage: Worldwide. The saved series runs from 1985 (from late 1989 for Ludhiana, whose first scene is 1 Nov 1989).
layers.canSay: Whether a pixel was green or bare on a clear day, and how a pixel's greenness in a season compares with its own other years.
layers.cannotSay: Which crop was growing, the edge of your field, or why a value is low: crop stress, a different crop, an early harvest and haze all look alike. Cloudy days are missing, not zero.
layers.statusText: Saved for the three demo pins (1985 to 2025); live Landsat read elsewhere.

cites.quote: NDVI is calculated from the visible and near-infrared light reflected by vegetation.
Landsat 8 images have 15-meter panchromatic and 30-meter multi-spectral spatial resolutions along a 185 km (115 mi) swath.
Has a 16-day repeat cycle with an equatorial crossing time of 10:12 a.m. +/- 5 minutes

cites.where: Sections 'What it is, and what it is not' and 'Saved data'

layers.name: MODIS greenness (NDVI), Brentwood only
layers.plain: A second satellite greenness record, much coarser than Landsat but with a steady 16-day schedule.
layers.resolution: 250 m pixel, one value per 16 days.
layers.coverage: Worldwide product. This app has saved MODIS only for Brentwood.
layers.canSay: A broad greenness pattern across an area.
layers.cannotSay: Anything about a single field smaller than a 250 m pixel.
layers.statusText: Brentwood only; other places show Landsat alone.

cites.quote: are generated every 16 days at 250 meter (m) spatial resolution as a Level 3 product.

layers.name: NASADEM ground height
layers.plain: A worldwide map of ground height, made from data of NASA's Shuttle Radar Topography Mission, used here for slope.
layers.canSay: Whether the ground around a pin is flat or sloping, at a 30 m scale.
layers.cannotSay: Slope on built-up or wooded ground: radar bounces off roofs and treetops. Ditches and field edges smaller than 30 m are not seen.
layers.statusText: Saved for the three demo pins; fetched live elsewhere.

cites.quote: NASADEM data products were derived from original telemetry data from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM)
30 Meters x 30 Meters

cites.where: Section 'Terrain: NASADEM' (it is a surface model; the Fresno pin is developed land)

layers.name: USDA Cropland Data Layer
layers.kindLabel: Satellite classification trained on ground records
layers.plain: A yearly USDA map of the crop probably growing on each pixel. It is made from satellite images and trained and checked with the Farm Service Agency's field records.
layers.resolution: 30 m pixels through 2023, 10 m from 2024. Yearly.
layers.coverage: Continental United States. This app uses 2008 to 2024.
layers.canSay: What the classification says a pixel was in each year, for example corn or developed land.
layers.cannotSay: Your own record. USDA gives 'generally 85% to 95%' producer's accuracy for the major crop categories, not for single pixels or field edges, and says pixel counts give biased area estimates.
layers.statusText: Saved for the three demo pins; Ludhiana is outside coverage.

cites.quote: is an annual raster, geo-referenced, crop-specific land cover data layer produced using satellite imagery.
Agricultural training and validation data are derived from the Farm Service Agency (FSA) Common Land Unit (CLU) Program.
The Producer's Accuracy is generally 85% to 95% correct for the major crop-specific land cover categories.
The CDL spatial resolution has been increased from 30-meter to 10-meter beginning in 2024.

layers.name: NLCD land cover
layers.plain: A national map of what covers the land (for example cropland, built-up, water), made from Landsat satellite images.
layers.coverage: United States. Ludhiana is outside coverage.
layers.canSay: The type of land cover at a point, for example that a pin is in a built-up class.
layers.cannotSay: Which crop, or how the land is managed.
layers.statusText: Saved for the three demo pins (NLCD 2021).

cites.quote: The National Land Cover Database (NLCD) serves as the definitive Landsat-based, 30-meter resolution, land cover database for the Nation.

layers.name: OpenET water use
layers.plain: A service that delivers satellite-based evapotranspiration (the water a real crop or ground cover uses) for a pixel.
layers.resolution: The documents read in this build give no explicit native pixel size, so none is stated here.
layers.coverage: Conterminous United States per the OpenET documents read in this build (docs/openet-check.md); the app's client refuses points outside it. Saved responses are included for Brentwood and Fresno only.
layers.canSay: What was actually growing and using water at the pixel, for comparison with the app's modelled crop.
layers.cannotSay: Whether the modelled crop is right: the pixel may hold a different crop, fallow land or not farmland.
layers.statusText: Saved response from 2026-11-16 for Brentwood and Fresno. The replay's How we know panel compares saved monthly actual water use with the modelled crop. A key is needed only to fetch new responses.

cites.quote: OpenET empowers water management from local to global scales by delivering transparent, scientifically rigorous satellite-based evapotranspiration (ET) data through accessible tools.

cites.where: Status line and 'What can and cannot be compared'

layers.name: SSURGO soil survey
layers.plain: The US national soil map database, collected by soil scientists over about a century. Each map area lists soil types and layers: sand, silt, clay, organic matter, pH and water capacity.
layers.resolution: Map scale between 1:12,000 and 1:63,360, so a map area, not a pixel.
layers.coverage: United States only. Ludhiana shows 'not available'.
layers.canSay: Typical soil texture, organic matter, water storage and erodibility for the soil type mapped at your pin.
layers.cannotSay: A test of your field. It has no plant-available nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium, and a map area mixes several soil types.
layers.statusText: Saved for the three demo pins; fetched live for other US places.

cites.quote: The Soil Survey Geographic Database (SSURGO) contains information about soil as collected by the National Cooperative Soil Survey over the course of a century.
The information was collected at scales ranging from 1:12,000 to 1:63,360.

cites.where: Section 'Soil: SSURGO via Soil Data Access'

layers.name: Daymet weather grid
layers.kindLabel: Map made from weather station records
layers.plain: A daily weather map of North America made by interpolating and extrapolating from weather station observations onto a 1 km grid.
layers.coverage: North America, Hawaii and Puerto Rico. Ludhiana has none.
layers.canSay: A finer, station-based picture of daily rain and temperature, used here as a second opinion on NASA POWER.
layers.cannotSay: Which of the two is right. The app compares two gridded products with each other; neither is a measurement at your farm.
layers.statusText: Saved for Brentwood and Fresno; Ludhiana is outside coverage.

cites.quote: The Daymet approach to estimating daily surface weather parameters at locations lacking instrumentation is based on a combination of interpolation and extrapolation, using inputs from multiple instrumented sites and weights for each site that reflect the spatial and temporal relationships of the estimation location to the instrumental observations.
produced on a 1 km x 1 km gridded surface
gridded estimates of daily weather parameters for North America, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico

cites.where: Framing rule and section 'Daymet V4 R1 (ORNL DAAC)'

layers.name: CoCoRaHS volunteer rain gauge
layers.plain: A network of volunteers who measure and map rain, hail and snow. The app checks one nearby gauge on the days it reported.
layers.resolution: One gauge: a single point, several kilometres from the grid squares.
layers.coverage: Only places the app has configured (Brentwood and Fresno).
layers.canSay: How much rain one gauge caught on the days it reported, which shows how far the gridded products can stray.
layers.cannotSay: Your field's rain, or a fair score for either grid. One gauge is indicative only, and a day with no report is skipped, never counted as dry.
layers.statusText: Saved for Brentwood and Fresno. Ludhiana: no station configured.

cites.quote: CoCoRaHS is a unique, non-profit, community-based network of volunteers of all ages and backgrounds working together to measure and map precipitation (rain, hail, and snow).

layers.name: USGS monitoring wells
layers.plain: Depth to water in monitoring wells, measured below the ground surface. The app shows the nearest well that has readings.
layers.coverage: United States and territories. Ludhiana has none within about 22 km.
layers.canSay: How deep the water was in that well when it was read.
layers.cannotSay: Your field's water table. It is a fact about that one well, and the newest reading may be years old.
layers.statusText: Saved for the three demo pins.

cites.quote: Data provided by the CRN form the basis for assessments and models that characterize the connections between climate and groundwater levels (depth to water below land surface).

layers.name: CIMIS weather station 47 (Brentwood)
layers.plain: California's network of automated weather stations. Station 47 at Brentwood reports hourly weather and an estimate of reference evapotranspiration for its own surroundings.
layers.resolution: One station: its own location and immediate surroundings.
layers.canSay: A real instrument's daily reference evapotranspiration, which the app compares with its own value computed from NASA POWER regional climate, about 50 km grid.
layers.cannotSay: Whether the regional estimate is correct at another farm. A station over irrigated grass and a 50 km grid square differ by nature; the reference-evapotranspiration methods also differ.
layers.statusText: Saved response from 2026-11-16 for station 47 at Brentwood. The replay's How we know panel computes the station comparison from the saved response. A key is needed only to fetch new responses.

cites.quote: CIMIS stations provide hourly records of solar radiation, precipitation, air temperature, air humidity, and wind speed.
Most of the CIMIS stations produce estimates of reference evapotranspiration (ETo) for the station location and their immediate surroundings, often in agricultural areas.

layers.name: SMAP surface soil moisture (SPL3SMP_E v006)
layers.plain: A NASA satellite that measures how much water is in the top layer of soil and produces global soil-moisture maps.
layers.resolution: Posted to a 9 km grid from an approximately 36 km radiometer footprint; approximately the top 5 cm of soil.
layers.coverage: Saved July 2025 snapshots for Brentwood, Fresno and Ludhiana only. Other locations are not fetched while the page loads.
layers.canSay: Surface soil moisture at the sampled grid cell on the saved dates. Only recommended-quality retrievals are displayed as moisture values.
layers.cannotSay: Root-zone water available to a crop, irrigation requirements, soil health, or conditions across an exact field boundary. A short snapshot does not establish a trend.
layers.statusText: Saved response from 2026-11-16 for the three demo pins. Observation dates and quality information are shown on the conditions page. The Earthdata token is used only by the fetch script. These observations do not change the water replay.

cites.quote: In ground that is not frozen or covered in water, SMAP measures how much water is in the top layer of soil, using this information to produce global maps of soil moisture.

cites.where: Products, quality handling, saved observations and real access findings

cites.quote: A retrieval_qual_flag value of either 0 or 8 indicates high-quality retrievals

layers.name: GPM IMERG Final monthly rainfall (v07)
layers.plain: A NASA product that merges rain estimates from many satellites into one continuous record. NASA says it is especially valuable where there are no ground instruments.
layers.coverage: Saved July 2025 snapshots for Brentwood, Fresno and Ludhiana only. Other locations are not fetched while the page loads.
layers.canSay: An estimated rainfall total for the sampled grid cell and saved month, calculated from the product's monthly mean rate with its uncertainty and quality fields retained.
layers.cannotSay: Rain measured on the farm, daily extremes within that month, future rainfall, or a 40-season trend from one month. It does not replace NASA POWER in the replay.
layers.statusText: Saved response from 2026-11-16 for the three demo pins. Observation dates and quality information are shown on the conditions page. The Earthdata token is used only by the fetch script. These observations do not change the water replay.

cites.quote: IMERG is particularly valuable over areas of Earth's surface that lack ground-based precipitation-measuring instruments, including oceans and remote areas.

cites.where: Products, quality handling, saved observations and real access findings

layers.name: ECOSTRESS surface temperature and water stress
layers.kindLabel: Satellite instrument on the space station
layers.plain: An instrument that takes high-resolution temperature images of the Earth's surface. NASA says plants with enough water keep their temperature, and plants short of water get warmer, and ECOSTRESS can measure that rise.
layers.resolution: Not stated here (not read in this build).
layers.coverage: Not stated here (not read in this build).
layers.statusText: Needs a free NASA Earthdata account and an access token, and this app has not been connected to one. No data are shown for it; nothing is estimated in its place.

cites.quote: ECOSTRESS acquires high resolution temperature and emissivity (composition) images of the Earth's surface.
If they have sufficient water they can maintain their temperature, but if there is insufficient water, their temperatures rise and this temperature rise can be measured with ECOSTRESS.

layers.name: GLDAS / NLDAS land models
layers.kindLabel: Land-surface model fed by satellite and ground data
layers.plain: NASA's Global Land Data Assimilation System: a land-surface model that takes in satellite and ground observations to produce estimates of soil moisture, runoff and similar quantities.
layers.resolution: Not stated here (not read in this build).
layers.statusText: Needs a free NASA Earthdata account and an access token, and this app has not been connected to one. No data are shown for it; nothing is estimated in its place.

cites.quote: The goal of the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) is to ingest satellite- and ground-based observational data products, using advanced land surface modeling and data assimilation techniques, in order to generate optimal fields of land surface states and fluxes

gaps: OpenET's native pixel size is not stated: the documents read give no explicit native-resolution sentence (docs/openet-check.md).
ECOSTRESS and GLDAS resolutions are not stated here because these later-stage layers are not implemented. SMAP and IMERG now have product-specific resolution and quality notes in docs/earthdata.md.
CoCoRaHS: the page read gives the network's purpose but not the instrument; the instrument is not described here.

CIMIS: the official CIMIS home page returned only its title and a UC Davis page returned an access-denied (HTTP 403) page, so the description comes from the California Department of Water Resources catalog record. It says 'over 145' active stations; older sources say over 120.
Daymet: its method description was read on the ORNL DAAC page. The app has not validated Daymet against anything; it only compares it with NASA POWER and one gauge.

NASA POWER's methodology page calls its weather data 'assimilation models' and does not use the word reanalysis; this app calls it reanalysis because MERRA-2, one of the models named, is described by NASA as a reanalysis.
NLCD: the exact citation of the 2021 dataset has not been confirmed from a page opened in this build (docs/ground-truth.md). The USGS page read also says part of it refers to the legacy NLCD.

Cropland Data Layer: pixels are 10 m from 2024, but the app samples a 3 by 3 block of points 30 m apart for every year. The app's own label and wording were corrected to say so on 2026-11-16; the saved data files still carry the older "30 m" source name.

Some quotations were copied from page text after the HTML tags were stripped, or from PDF text extraction (a line break was removed in one soil-column quote). Quotes were not re-checked against a second fetch.
